cities.metaDescription: Montevideo, Uruguay real estate 2026: equal rights for foreigners, ~$2,840/m² median asking, 5–6% gross yields, closing costs and the new-resident tax holiday.
about: Montevideo draws foreign buyers with a legal system that treats them like locals and a market priced in US dollars. Uruguay's investment law (Law 16.906) gives foreign investors the same treatment as nationals, and anyone, national or foreign, can own real estate. In the Índice INGAR for September 2026, the median asking price for apartments across Montevideo's barrios was about $2,840/m², rising to $3,956 in Pocitos, $4,184 in Punta Carretas and $4,370 in Carrasco. Estimated gross yields ran about 5–5.5% in those prime areas and 6.2% in Cordón and Centro. Since January 1, 2026, people who become tax residents can choose to pay non-resident income tax (IRNR) instead of IRPF on foreign investment income for the year they arrive plus the next ten. That applies if they spend more than 183 days a year in Uruguay or meet an investment test, such as more than UI 12.5 million in real estate, and were not tax residents in the previous two years.

The purchase runs through an escribano público, a notary chosen by the buyer. The escribano studies the title, drafts the escritura (deed), withholds the taxes and registers the first copy of the deed at the Registro de la Propiedad, Sección Inmobiliaria. That registry is run by the Dirección General de Registros and organised by the department where the property sits. Typical buyer costs are a notary fee of about 3% plus 22% VAT, an agent's commission of 3% plus VAT if an agent is involved, and the 2% property transfer tax (ITP). The seller pays another 2% ITP. ITP is charged on the cadastral value, which is usually well below the market price, so one Montevideo law firm estimates total buyer costs at 5–9% of the price.

The main risks are crime, cost and thin data. The US State Department rates Uruguay Level 2, 'Exercise increased caution', because of crime, in an advisory issued July 28, 2026. It says homicide, armed robbery, carjacking and theft are most common in Montevideo, Canelones, Maldonado and Rivera. Price and yield figures come from asking prices, not closed sales, and gross yields fall once tax, vacancy, management and building fees are counted. Montevideo is also expensive for the region: Numbeo puts a single person's monthly costs at about $980 before rent.

faq.q: Can foreigners buy property in Montevideo, Uruguay?
faq.a: Yes, on the same terms as Uruguayans. Law 16.906 gives foreign investors the same treatment as nationals, and anyone, national or foreign, can own and occupy real estate.

faq.q: What are the closing costs when buying in Montevideo?
faq.a: Buyers typically pay a notary fee of about 3% plus 22% VAT, an agent's commission of 3% plus VAT if an agent is involved, and 2% property transfer tax (ITP) on the cadastral value, plus small title-study and registration fees. One Montevideo law firm puts the total at 5–9% of the price.

faq.q: Does Uruguay still have a 10-year tax holiday for new residents?
faq.a: In a changed form. For people who become tax residents from January 1, 2026, Law 20.446 lets them pay non-resident income tax (IRNR) instead of IRPF on foreign investment income for the year they become resident plus ten more. To qualify they must spend more than 183 days a year in Uruguay or invest more than UI 12.5 million in real estate or at least UI 625,000 a year in qualifying funds, and must not have been tax residents in the previous two years. Confirm your case with a Uruguayan tax adviser.

faq.q: Is Montevideo safe for foreign property buyers?
faq.a: The US State Department rates Uruguay Level 2, 'Exercise increased caution', because of crime, in its July 28, 2026 advisory. It names Montevideo among the departments where crime is most common, with homicide, armed robbery, carjacking and theft the main concerns.

cities.tagline: Pacific clifftop capital — foreigners own on equal terms, and prime districts ask about $2,500/m².
cities.metaDescription: Lima, Peru real estate 2026 — Miraflores, Barranco, San Isidro prices, rental yields, foreign ownership rules and cost of living.
about: Lima is a metropolitan area of about 10 million people, and most foreign buyers focus on the ocean-side districts of Miraflores, Barranco and San Isidro. Peru's Constitution (Article 71) puts foreigners on the same footing as Peruvians for property ownership, so you can buy in your own name with no residency, local partner or trust. The restriction applies only within 50 km of the country's borders, far from Lima. Central bank (BCRP) data put median asking prices in Q1 2026 at about US$2,460 per square meter in Miraflores, US$2,560 in Barranco and US$2,600 in San Isidro, and dollar prices rose about 10–21% over the previous year.

Ownership is transferred by a public deed (escritura pública) signed before a notary and then registered with SUNARP, the public registry. SUNARP stresses that the deed alone is not enough: register the sale, check the registry certificate before you buy, and ask the notary for a registry block until signing. The buyer pays the 3% alcabala transfer tax on the value above 10 UIT (S/ 55,000 in 2026). A non-resident individual landlord pays a 5% tax on gross rent, which a domiciled tenant withholds.

The risks are real. The US State Department rates Peru Level 2, 'Exercise increased caution', citing crime, unrest, kidnapping and terrorism, and Lima and Callao have been under repeated states of emergency since September 2024 over killings and extortion. Lima sits in a major earthquake zone, and the civil defence agency INDECI warns of a possible magnitude 8.8 quake off the central coast, so check a building's age and its compliance with the E.030 seismic code. Politics are volatile: Keiko Fujimori's July 2026 inauguration was Peru's ninth change of president in ten years. Gross yields are moderate, at about 5.5–6%, and published prices are asking prices, so budget time and negotiating room for resale.

faq.q: Can foreigners buy property in Lima, Peru?
faq.a: Yes. Article 71 of Peru's Constitution gives foreigners the same property rights as Peruvians, so you can buy an apartment in Lima in your own name with no residency or local partner. The only restriction is within 50 km of the borders, which does not affect Lima.

faq.q: How much does an apartment cost per square meter in Miraflores?
faq.a: BCRP data put the median asking price at about US$2,460 per square meter in Miraflores in Q1 2026, with San Isidro at about US$2,600 and Barranco about US$2,560. Urbania's July 2026 index had Miraflores at S/ 8,905 per square meter.

faq.q: What rental yield can I expect in Lima?
faq.a: About 5.5–6% gross. BCRP price-to-rent ratios for Q1 2026 imply about 5.6% in Miraflores and 6.0% in San Isidro, and Urbania put Lima's average at 5.53% in July 2026. Non-resident landlords pay a 5% tax on gross rent.

faq.q: What taxes do I pay when buying property in Lima?
faq.a: The buyer pays the alcabala transfer tax: 3% of the value above 10 UIT, or above S/ 55,000 in 2026. In the province of Lima it is paid to SAT Lima by the last business day of the month after the transfer.

cities.tagline: Santa Catarina's island capital: beach neighbourhoods, prices up 8% in a year, and title quirks on federal coastal land.
cities.metaDescription: Florianópolis, Brazil real estate 2026: FipeZap prices near R$13,600/m², 5.4% gross yields, CPF, escritura, 2% ITBI and terreno de marinha rules for foreigners.
about: Florianópolis, the capital of Santa Catarina, is split between Santa Catarina Island and a mainland district, and had 537,211 residents in the 2022 Census. Foreign interest centres on the island's beach neighbourhoods, such as Jurerê, Canasvieiras, Ingleses and Armação, and on Lagoa da Conceição; the state government notes heavy summer tourism, much of it from Argentina. It is not cheap: in September 2026 the FipeZap index put the average residential asking price at R$13,607/m², up 8.3% in 12 months, the second highest of the state capitals it tracks after Vitória and well above the R$10,015/m² index average. FipeZap's gross long-term rental yield for the city was about 5.4% a year.

Foreigners can buy urban property in their own name; rural land is subject to a separate regime under Law 5.709/1971, which caps foreign holdings at a quarter of a municipality's area. You first need a CPF tax number, which non-residents request free of charge at a Brazilian consulate. Above 30 times the minimum wage, the Civil Code requires the sale to be made by escritura pública, signed at a tabelionato de notas, and ownership only passes when that deed is registered at the Cartório de Registro de Imóveis; until then the seller is still the legal owner. Florianópolis charges ITBI transfer tax at 2% under its tax code (art. 285-A), with 0.5% on the part financed through the SFH housing system up to an inflation-indexed cap.

Two local issues need a lawyer's check. Much of the shoreline is terreno de marinha: Union land within 33 m of the 1831 mean high-tide line, including around islands, managed by the SPU. Holders pay an annual fee (0.6% of land value for aforamento), and the seller pays the Union a 5% laudêmio on the land value when it is sold. A 2018 press report counted about 42,000 such plots in the city, 39,000 not yet finally demarcated. Federal law also protects mangroves, restingas and a 30 m strip around natural lakes in urban zones, and courts have blocked new building permits in protected areas such as Praia Brava. Prices are in reais, so returns move with the exchange rate, and there is no reliable published data on short-term rental returns.

faq.q: Can foreigners buy property in Florianópolis?
faq.a: Yes. Urban property can be bought in a foreigner's own name; rural land falls under Law 5.709/1971, which limits foreign ownership. You need a Brazilian CPF tax number, which non-residents get free at a Brazilian consulate, before you sign.

faq.q: What taxes do you pay when buying in Florianópolis?
faq.a: The municipality charges ITBI transfer tax at 2% (0.5% on the part financed through the SFH, up to a cap). If the property is on federal coastal land (terreno de marinha), the seller also pays the Union a 5% laudêmio on the land value, and the owner pays an annual fee to the SPU. Notary and registry fees come on top.

faq.q: What is a terreno de marinha and why does it matter?
faq.a: It is federal land within 33 m of the 1831 mean high-tide line, along the coast and around islands, managed by the SPU. You hold use rights rather than full ownership, pay an annual fee and owe laudêmio on resale. A 2018 press report counted about 42,000 such plots in Florianópolis, so ask your lawyer to check the SPU status of any coastal property.

faq.q: What rental yield can I expect in Florianópolis?
faq.a: FipeZap put the gross long-term rental yield at about 5.4% a year in September 2026, based on asking rents and prices, before taxes, vacancy and costs. There is no reliable published data for short-term holiday rental returns.

cities.tagline: One of Central America's oldest colonial cities — low prices, but seizures of foreign-owned property make it a high-risk buy.
cities.metaDescription: Granada, Nicaragua real estate 2026: foreign buyer rules, title and confiscation risks, the 2025 constitution, thin price data and the US travel advisory.
about: Granada, on the shore of Lake Nicaragua, is one of Central America's oldest colonial cities, and its restored courtyard houses are what draw most foreign buyers. Foreigners can buy property here in their own name: The US State Department reports no specific restrictions on foreign or non-resident investors apart from border and national-security areas, and a standard purchase needs no residency permit, local partner or minimum investment. The 2025 constitution protects property in Article 40 but allows expropriation 'with fair compensation', and the same State Department report documents seizures of foreign-owned property. In August 2026 the government took nine homes owned by US retirees in Tola, Rivas; eight were returned in October.

The real work is the title. Purchases are signed as an escritura pública before a Nicaraguan notary and then entered in the Registro Público under Law 698 of 2009. The US Embassy estimates about 28,000 properties were confiscated between 1979 and 1990 and many remain disputed, and colonial houses tend to have the longest ownership chains, so a full title study by your own lawyer is essential before any deposit.

Buyers should also weigh the political backdrop. As of May 2026 the US State Department rates Nicaragua Level 3, 'Reconsider travel', citing crime, limited healthcare, wrongful detention and other risks. Granada's prices are low by regional standards, but liquidity is thinner than in Costa Rica or Panama, so plan for a longer hold and a slower resale.

faq.q: Can foreigners buy property in Granada, Nicaragua?
faq.a: Legally, yes. The US State Department reports no specific restrictions on foreign or non-resident buyers apart from border and national-security areas, including a 15 km strip along land borders declared state property in 2025. But the same report says the government has seized foreign-owned property, so treat any purchase as high-risk.

faq.q: What is the biggest risk when buying in Granada?
faq.a: Title history. The US Embassy estimates around 28,000 properties were confiscated between 1979 and 1990 and many are still disputed. Hire your own lawyer, order a full title study at the Registro Público, and never rely on an unregistered deed.

faq.q: Is it safe to buy property in Nicaragua right now?
faq.a: The US State Department rated Nicaragua Level 3, 'Reconsider travel', in its May 2026 advisory, citing crime, limited healthcare and the risk of wrongful detention. In August 2026 the government also took nine homes owned by US retirees in Tola, Rivas, so it is a much higher-risk market than Costa Rica or Panama.

faq.q: Can I get residency in Nicaragua as a retiree?
faq.a: Possibly, but the rules changed: the old pensionado law (Law 694) was repealed by the 2024 General Tourism Law (Law 1210), and retiree residency now falls under the general migration law. Confirm the current requirements and income threshold with the Dirección General de Migración y Extranjería or an immigration lawyer before applying.

cities.metaDescription: San Juan del Sur, Nicaragua real estate 2026: asking prices, coastal-zone law 690, title and confiscation risks, border-strip rules and the US travel advisory.
about: San Juan del Sur is a small Pacific bay town in Nicaragua's Rivas department, and its surf beaches and ocean-view hillsides are what draw most foreign buyers. Homes and condos are listed in US dollars: asking prices on Encuentra24 run from roughly US$1,000 per square metre for modest houses to about US$2,600 at the top end for beachfront condos. Foreigners can hold title in their own name: the US State Department reports no specific restrictions on foreign buyers outside border and national-security areas, and the 2025 constitution protects property in Article 40 while allowing expropriation 'with fair compensation'; the same report documents seizures of foreign-owned property, and in August 2026 the government took nine homes owned by US retirees in nearby Tola.

Coastal land has its own rules. Under Ley 690 of 2009, the Coastal Zones Development Law, the beach between low and high tide plus 50 metres inland from the average high-tide mark is state-owned public-use land where homes are prohibited, and the next 200 metres inland is a restricted zone where the state regulates use. Neither strip can be sold, only granted by concession, although rights legally acquired before the law and already-established urban centres are exempt. Purchases are recorded in the Registro Público de la Propiedad, part of the national registry system set up by Law 698 of 2009. The US Embassy says about 28,000 properties were expropriated between 1979 and 1990, many are still disputed, and it urges extreme caution with coastal property in particular.

The country risk is real. The US State Department rates Nicaragua Level 3, 'Reconsider travel', citing crime, health, wrongful detention and arbitrary enforcement of local laws. In August 2025 the National Assembly passed Law 1258, which declares a 15-kilometre strip along Nicaragua's borders state property, and the State Department called it a 'massive confiscation'. The town itself is roughly 25–30 km from the Costa Rican border, outside the strip, but the municipality's southern beaches (El Ostional, La Flor, Playa El Coco) lie within or close to it, so have a lawyer confirm where any lot sits. Nicaragua publishes no sales-price data and no reliable rental-yield figures, so treat agents' yield claims with caution and plan for a long hold.

faq.q: Can foreigners buy beachfront property in San Juan del Sur?
faq.a: Foreigners can own private land in their own name, but not the beach itself. Ley 690 makes the area between the tides plus 50 metres inland from the average high-tide mark public-use state land where homes are banned, and the next 200 metres inland is a restricted zone. Rights legally acquired before 2009 are respected, so your lawyer must check exactly where any lot sits.

faq.q: How much does property cost in San Juan del Sur?
faq.a: There is no official price index. Asking prices on Encuentra24 in 2026 range from about US$1,000 per square metre for modest houses to about US$2,600 at the top end for beachfront condos. Treat these as asking prices, not sale prices.

faq.q: What are the biggest risks of buying in San Juan del Sur?
faq.a: Title and politics. The US Embassy says about 28,000 properties were expropriated in 1979-1990, many are still disputed, and it urges extreme caution with coastal property. Law 1258 of 2025 also made a 15 km strip along Nicaragua's borders state property: the town is outside it, but the southern beaches such as El Ostional, La Flor and Playa El Coco are within or close to it. Order a full title study at the Registro Público before paying any deposit.

faq.q: Is it safe to buy property in Nicaragua right now?
faq.a: The US State Department rates Nicaragua Level 3, 'Reconsider travel', citing crime, health, wrongful detention and arbitrary enforcement of local laws, and the US Embassy urges extreme caution when buying coastal property. Weigh that risk, and the slow resale market, before committing.
